drills.q: Explain the open-model vs closed-model distinction in load testing, and give an example of when each is the correct choice.
drills.a: Open model: requests arrive at a rate independent of system response time (Poisson process, exponential inter-arrival) -- correct for public, unauthenticated, arrival-driven traffic like a public API or marketing site, since a slow system there experiences real, unbounded queue buildup as new users keep arriving. Closed model: a fixed number of virtual users loop request-wait-response-repeat, so a slowing system causes each user's effective request rate to drop, making throughput look artificially stable -- correct for genuinely bounded populations, like an internal tool used by exactly 500 named employees who cannot exceed that concurrency.

drills.q: A load test script sends the next request the instant the previous response arrives, with no delay. What's wrong with this, mechanically?
drills.a: It eliminates think time, which massively overstates each simulated user's real request rate. A real user issuing roughly one request every several seconds gets modeled as issuing requests as fast as the network allows -- requiring far fewer virtual users to reach a target aggregate throughput than reality would need, and consequently testing a fundamentally different connection/concurrency scenario (unrealistic per-connection request rate) rather than realistic user behavior.

drills.q: Why is a fixed, uniform sleep() between requests still an inadequate model of think time, even though it's better than no delay at all?
drills.a: Real user pauses follow a right-skewed (log-normal) distribution -- most users pause a typical amount, but a real tail of users pauses much longer. A uniform fixed delay smooths out this variance, eliminating the burst/lull pattern real traffic has, which understates the tail behavior that often drives real system stress (e.g., a burst of near-simultaneous requests after a batch of users all finish a similar-length pause).

drills.q: A load test 'passes' cleanly at high sustained throughput on a single endpoint, but production falls over at a fraction of that load under real usage. Diagnose the likely test-design flaw.
drills.a: The test was almost certainly closed-model with zero think time against one endpoint in isolation, which measures the load generator/endpoint's raw throughput ceiling rather than realistic concurrent-user behavior across a real traffic mix. Fix: rebuild as an open-model (arrival-rate) test with realistic think time and a weighted multi-endpoint mix derived from actual production traffic logs, so shared resources (connection pools, caches, downstream services) are stressed the way they would be in reality.

drills.q: Why should JMeter's actual load-generation runs always be executed via CLI (non-GUI) mode, and what goes wrong if you don't?
drills.a: JMeter's GUI is a heavyweight Java Swing application that does live rendering and listener updates during the test; this competes with the load generator itself for CPU and memory, producing both lower achievable throughput and less trustworthy latency numbers than the same plan run headless. Build the test plan visually in the GUI, but execute real load runs with `jmeter -n -t plan.jmx -l results.jtl`.

drills.q: In k6's ramping-arrival-rate executor, what's the difference between preAllocatedVUs and maxVUs, and what does it mean operationally if a test run hits maxVUs?
drills.a: preAllocatedVUs is the pool of virtual users k6 starts with to sustain the target arrival rate; maxVUs is a hard ceiling k6 can grow into if responses slow down and more concurrent VUs are needed to keep the arrival rate constant. Hitting maxVUs during a run is itself a finding: it means the system under test cannot sustain that arrival rate without unbounded concurrency/queue growth -- the correct response is to investigate why, not simply raise the ceiling and rerun.

drills.q: A load test shows near-100% cache hit rate and low latency at a given throughput; production shows 60% hit rate and much higher latency at the same throughput. What's the likely test flaw and the fix?
drills.a: The test almost certainly reused a small, fixed set of request parameters (the same handful of product IDs or search queries) repeatedly, giving the cache an artificially easy workload. Real traffic has a much wider access distribution, often Zipfian-skewed (a few popular items, a long tail of rarely-requested ones); sampling request parameters from a distribution matching real access patterns -- not a fixed small set, and not necessarily uniform random either -- reproduces realistic cache-miss behavior.

drills.q: Explain why testing only a gradual ramp, or only a step-function spike, each miss a distinct real failure mode, and give a production scenario each would catch that the other wouldn't.
drills.a: A step-function ramp (instant jump to target load) stresses simultaneous connection setup, TLS handshakes, and cold caches -- it catches burst-driven failures like a flash-sale traffic spike or a viral link overwhelming connection pools all at once. A gradual ramp stresses organic growth -- it catches degradation that only appears under sustained load, like a memory leak that manifests after tens of minutes, or an autoscaling policy that reacts too slowly. Running only one misses the failure mode specific to the other.

drills.q: When would choosing Gatling over k6 for a new load-testing initiative be a mistake despite Gatling's superior per-machine throughput and reporting?
drills.a: When the team maintaining the tests has no Scala/JVM background and a tight deadline -- Gatling's Scala DSL has a real learning curve, and a load-testing practice only one Scala-literate engineer can read or extend becomes a bus-factor risk and a black box to the rest of the team. In that context, k6 (JavaScript) or Locust (Python), written and maintained by the whole team, is the more durable choice even at somewhat lower per-agent efficiency.

drills.q: Your team runs a 2-minute k6 load test on every PR and it has never failed a threshold, yet production has had three load-related incidents this year. Diagnose and propose a plan.
drills.a: A 2-minute test cannot surface the failure modes actually responsible for those incidents -- connection pool exhaustion under sustained load, memory growth that only appears after tens of minutes (soak-test territory), or a genuine capacity breakpoint well above the load a short smoke-style test reaches. The team is likely treating a fast PR-gate regression check as their entire performance-testing practice. Plan: keep the fast per-PR test for catching obvious immediate regressions, and add a separate, less frequent (nightly/pre-release) test program covering soak, spike, and breakpoint scenarios against realistic traffic models -- don't try to make the PR-gate test longer, since that destroys development velocity for a benefit better achieved with a properly scoped separate cadence.
